samples.summary: Connector still hand-builds `<a:ln>` instead of reusing `lineXml` — the duplication that caused this very bug is left in place
samples.evidence: `connectorToXml` assembles `<a:ln w="${lnW}">${fillXml}${dash}${headXml}${tailXml}</a:ln>` (connector.ts:140), which is byte-for-byte the string `lineXml` produces in shape.ts:139 (`<a:ln w="${w}">${fill}${dash}${head}${tail}</a:ln>`; `pxToEmu` and `pxToEmuX` are the same function today, units.ts:10-19). The missing connector dash this delta fixes is exactly the failure mode of having two `<a:ln>` serializers: the shape one learned `prstDash`, the connector one did not. The delta patches the symptom (share `dashXml`) rather than the cause; the next line property (`cap`, `cmpd`, gradient line fill) will diverge the same way. The cycle the docstring cites (shape.ts → connector.ts) is itself the signal that line serialization wants its own module (e.g. `export/pptx/line.ts` holding `arrowXml`/`dashXml`/`lineXml`), which both shape and connector could then import.

samples.summary: `DASH_VAL`/`dashXml` — a generic line-property mapping — is homed in the connector module and imported back into shape.ts
samples.evidence: shape.ts:7 now does `import { arrowXml, dashXml } from './connector.js'` for a helper that has nothing to do with connectors; the docstring (connector.ts:86-88) admits the placement is dictated only by avoiding an import cycle. Layering by "whichever file already imports the other" is how connector.ts accretes shared line concerns; the neutral home is a line/stroke module (see the duplication finding above).

samples.summary: Design doc now states the opposite of the shipped behavior: "a 16px dashed border previews as one long block"
samples.evidence: slides-toolbar-redesign.md:187-195 — updated by an earlier round of this same PR — argues the 3px clamp was deleted because the picker must be honest, and concludes "The honest consequence: a 16px dashed border previews as one long block, because that is what it is." This delta's `fitPattern` (stroke-preview.tsx:26-31) deliberately prevents that: at 16px the dashed pattern is rescaled to fit two cycles in 64px, so the preview shows a short dash rhythm, not one long block. The canonical doc for this control now documents behavior the code no longer has, and CLAUDE.md/CONTRIBUTING require the design doc to move with the change.

samples.summary: `fitPattern` reinstates the "flattering picker" the clamp was deleted for, by a different mechanism
samples.evidence: The rationale recorded for removing `DASH_PREVIEW_MAX_WEIGHT` was that a 16px dashed border genuinely reads as long blocks, so a preview that hides this is flattering rather than accurate (stroke-preview.tsx:51-57 and slides-toolbar-redesign.md:187-195). `fitPattern` now rescales the pattern so the 16px Dashed row shows a short, clearly-dashed rhythm the canvas will not paint at that weight — the same user-facing dishonesty, relocated from the weight axis to the pattern axis. A preview that is a *scaled window* of the real line (shrink weight and pattern together via the viewBox) would keep both honest; the chosen split keeps one dimension true and the other invented. Judgement call, but it contradicts the stated design principle in the same file's own docstring ("cannot drift from what the slide canvas strokes", now weakened to "its shape cannot drift").

samples.summary: Now-shared `dashXml` not applied to table cell borders, which carry `CellBorder.dash` and render dashed on canvas
samples.evidence: `model/element.ts:435` gives `CellBorder` a `dash` field and `table-renderer.ts:314` honors it via `dashArray`, but `table.ts:120` emits `<a:ln${side} w="…">${solidFillXml(color)}</a:ln${side}>` with no `<a:prstDash>` (and the importer's `parseCellBorder` reads none either). With `dashXml` now extracted precisely so every `<a:ln>` producer can share it, the table exporter is the one remaining producer that silently drops dash. Arguably outside this PR's scope (no UI sets table-border dash today), but worth a deliberate decision rather than an omission.
